keyVerseText: And some of the chief of the fathers gave unto the work. The Tirshatha gave to the treasure a thousand drams of gold, fifty basons, five hundred and thirty priests' garments. some: Heb. part.
rootMeaning: The root of קְצָת (qᵉtsâth) is קָצָה (qâtsâh), which carries the idea of cutting off, cutting short, or scraping off. This root suggests a sense of limitation or boundary—something that marks an end or a portion separated from the whole. Understanding this root enriches the common English gloss of "end" or "part" by highlighting the notion of a distinct termination or a segment that has been deliberately separated or set apart.
usageInScripture: This word appears five times in Scripture and is consistently associated with the concepts of 'end,' 'part,' or 'some,' often indicating a portion or a boundary. Translations range from phrases like 'And some of,' 'with part,' to temporal markers such as 'that at the end' or 'Now at the end,' showing its flexible use both spatially and temporally. This range reveals that qᵉtsâth encompasses both physical ends (such as corners or edges) and figurative ends (such as portions or times), emphasizing the idea of a defined segment within a larger context.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, qᵉtsâth reminds believers that God’s providence and redemptive work often unfold within appointed boundaries and portions of time and space. The concept of an 'end' or 'part' aligns with biblical themes of God’s sovereign control over beginnings and endings, as well as the distribution of blessings and responsibilities among His people. Recognizing the root meaning of cutting off or setting apart enriches our understanding of how God separates and sanctifies His people and moments for His purposes. This word encourages faith in God's precise and purposeful ordering of history and individual lives, assuring us that nothing is random but divinely measured and appointed.
keyVerseReflection: In Nehemiah 7:70, the phrase 'And some of the chief of the fathers gave unto the work' uses qᵉtsâth to convey a portion or part given toward a sacred task. Here, the word highlights the act of contributing a distinct segment of resources, symbolizing willing participation in God’s work. This usage underscores the faithfulness of God’s people in dedicating their 'part' to the rebuilding effort, reminding us that every contribution, no matter the size, is meaningful within the community of faith.
